questions.q: What distinguishes a formal data quality rule from an ad-hoc query?
options: A rule is documented so it can run repeatedly with a known meaning on failure, including scope, severity, and an owner
A rule must use a JOIN; a query never does
A rule can only check one column, while a query can check many
There is no real difference — the terms are interchangeable
questions.explain: The SQL can be identical; what makes it a rule is the documentation around it — scope, condition, severity, and owner — that lets anyone run it and understand a failure.

questions.q: What are the four parts of a well-documented data quality rule, per this lesson?
options: Scope, condition, severity, and owner
Table, column, index, and primary key
Accuracy, completeness, consistency, and validity
SELECT, FROM, WHERE, and GROUP BY
questions.explain: Scope defines what's covered, condition defines pass/fail, severity defines urgency, and owner defines who's responsible for acting on failures.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say skipping the 'severity' part of a rule is a problem?
options: Without severity, every failure looks equally urgent, making it hard to prioritize
SQL Server will reject a query that has no severity comment
Severity is required for a query to use a JOIN
Severity determines which database the rule runs against
questions.explain: Severity (Critical/Warning/Informational) lets a team distinguish urgent failures from minor ones; without it, all failures appear equally important.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a failed accuracy rule can only be detected, never auto-prevented, while a failed validity rule sometimes can be?
options: Accuracy depends on real-world truth outside the database, while validity is a rule the database itself can enforce (e.g. with a CHECK constraint)
Accuracy rules are always slower to run than validity rules
Validity rules cannot be written as SQL queries
Accuracy can only be checked on weekends
questions.explain: Validity is about conforming to a defined rule, which a CHECK constraint can enforce at write time. Accuracy is about matching external truth, which the database has no way to verify or prevent automatically.

questions.q: In the example rule's SQL comment header (RULE, SCOPE, SEVERITY, OWNER), what purpose does this header serve when the rule is later automated?
options: It becomes the basis for the automated job's name, description, and alert routing
It has no further purpose once the rule is written
It replaces the need for the actual SELECT query
It is only used for SQL Server's query optimizer
questions.explain: The lesson explains that when the rule is automated (Lesson 22), the documented header becomes the job's name, description, and who gets alerted on failure.
